title: Heartland & Rimland Theory
description: Mackinder, Spykman, and the geographical logic of great-power competition

concepts.title: What Geopolitics Is
concepts.contentHtml:
Geopolitics in its classical sense is the study of how geography — distance, terrain, sea access, climate, the distribution of resources — shapes the strategic options of states. The term was coined in 1899 by the Swedish political scientist Rudolf Kjellén, though the underlying intuition is much older: Thucydides on the consequences of Athenian sea power, Ibn Khaldun on the desert and the city, Machiavelli on terrain.

The early-20th-century geopoliticians treated geography as a permanent backdrop against which great-power competition played out. Mountains, rivers, coastlines, and chokepoints did not change with regimes; they constrained even the most ambitious leaders. The geographical pivot of the world, the great rimlands, the maritime chokepoints — these were treated as structural facts the strategist had to read.

Modern geopolitics is more chastened about geographical determinism. Technology, demography, ideology, and economic interdependence all change what geography means in any given era: the airplane, the ICBM, the internet, and the container ship have all altered the strategic significance of distance. But the core insight — that the world's coastlines, mountain ranges, and resource maps shape the menu of options statesmen face — has survived the criticisms and remains a working framework for analysing great-power competition.

concepts.title: Mackinder's Heartland Theory
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential geopolitical theory of the 20th century is Halford Mackinder's. The British geographer's 1904 lecture "The Geographical Pivot of History," expanded into Democratic Ideals and Reality (1919), argued that the inner core of Eurasia — the "Heartland" — was the strategic key to the world.

Mackinder's reasoning ran roughly as follows. The world's largest landmass, the "World-Island" of Eurasia plus Africa, contains most of the world's population and resources. The Heartland — broadly modern Russia and Central Asia — is the inner zone, accessible only by land and protected from sea power. Whoever controls the Heartland can deny others access to its resources, build land power without the constraint of naval blockade, and ultimately dominate the World-Island. His often-quoted formulation: "Who rules East Europe commands the Heartland; who rules the Heartland commands the World-Island; who rules the World-Island commands the world."

Mackinder wrote with Russia in mind, then Germany, then both. His theory shaped early-20th-century British and later American strategic thinking. The architects of US containment in the late 1940s — Kennan, Acheson, the early planners of NATO and the Marshall Plan — operated within a framework recognisably descended from Mackinder. The contemporary revival of the framework, in light of Russia's behaviour in Ukraine and Chinese investment across Eurasia, is one of the reasons Mackinder is still widely read.

concepts.title: Spykman's Rimland and the Cold War Consensus
concepts.contentHtml:
The Dutch-American geopolitician Nicholas Spykman (America's Strategy in World Politics, 1942; The Geography of the Peace, 1944) reframed Mackinder's argument. Spykman accepted that Eurasia was the strategic centre of the world but argued that the decisive zone was not the inner Heartland but the Rimland — the long crescent of densely populated coastal regions stretching from Western Europe through the Middle East to South and East Asia.

Spykman's reasoning: the Rimland was where land power and sea power intersected; it contained most of the world's industrial capacity, population, and accessible resources; and it was the zone any aspiring hegemon — Russian or German or Japanese — would have to control to dominate the world-island. His reformulation: "Who controls the Rimland rules Eurasia; who rules Eurasia controls the destinies of the world."

Cold War US grand strategy can be read as Spykman's framework in action. Containment, articulated by George Kennan in his 1946 "Long Telegram" and 1947 "X article," prescribed sustained pressure along the Soviet periphery — Western Europe, Greece, Turkey, the Persian Gulf, Korea, Japan — precisely the Rimland zones. NATO, the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, and the Asian alliance system were all instruments of holding the Rimland against Soviet pressure into the Heartland. Whatever one thinks of the strategy's individual choices — Vietnam being the most contested — the geographical logic underlying it was substantially Spykman's.

title: Sea Power & Maritime Strategy
description: Mahan, choke points, blue-water navies — control of the global commons

concepts.title: Mahan and the Influence of Sea Power
concepts.contentHtml:
The most influential American strategic thinker of the late 19th century was the naval officer Alfred Thayer Mahan, whose The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890) argued that maritime nations had repeatedly outcompeted continental rivals, and that sea power was the decisive instrument of world-historical primacy.

Mahan's argument had several components. Trade and prosperity depend on the sea-lanes; controlling those lanes generates the wealth needed to sustain military power. A great navy requires a chain of overseas bases for coaling, supply, and forward presence. Decisive battles between major fleets — the "fleet in being" aside — establish maritime dominance. The British example since the 17th century, on Mahan's reading, was the textbook of how sea power had built a global empire.

Mahan's book was read by President Theodore Roosevelt, who used it to justify the 1898 acquisition of overseas territories and the construction of the Great White Fleet; by Imperial Japan, which built up the Combined Fleet; and by Wilhelmine Germany, where Tirpitz's naval-building programme — pursuing "risk theory" — explicitly cited Mahan. The naval-arms race that followed contributed materially to the international tensions that produced the First World War. Mahan's analytic framework reshaped great-power strategy across continents in barely a generation.

concepts.title: Maritime Chokepoints and the Global Commons
concepts.contentHtml:
The world's oceans are mostly empty; the strategic action is concentrated at chokepoints — narrow passages where shipping is forced through corridors a navy can plausibly control. The major chokepoints have shaped world politics for centuries.

  • The Strait of Hormuz (between Iran and Oman) carries roughly 20% of global oil exports and is the most-discussed chokepoint of the 21st century.
  • The Strait of Malacca (between Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore) is the world's busiest shipping lane by tonnage; the "Malacca Dilemma" is China's recognition that 80% of its energy imports pass through a strait dominated by US and allied naval forces.
  • The Bab-el-Mandeb, between the Horn of Africa and Yemen, is the southern entrance to the Red Sea–Suez route; Houthi attacks on shipping after October 2023 illustrated how a regional militia can disrupt global commerce.
  • The Suez and Panama canals are man-made chokepoints that connect oceans.
  • The Bosphorus and Dardanelles, governed by Turkey under the 1936 Montreux Convention, control Russian access to the Mediterranean.
  • The Greenland-Iceland-UK Gap remains the strategic chokepoint between the North Atlantic and the Russian Northern Fleet's home waters.

Sea power, in this picture, is largely the ability to control or contest these passages. The US Navy's global posture — eleven supercarriers, a worldwide network of bases, freedom-of-navigation operations — is structured around this logic. The contemporary great-power competition with China is partly a contest about whether the US can preserve the open commons regime through which global trade flows.

concepts.title: From Blue-Water Navies to A2/AD
concepts.contentHtml:
A "blue-water navy" — capable of sustained operations across deep oceans — is in 2026 a club of perhaps half a dozen members: the US, China, the UK, France, India, Russia (with significant constraints), and arguably Japan. Most other nations operate "green-water" (regional) or "brown-water" (coastal) forces. Building and sustaining a blue-water capability is one of the most expensive things a state can attempt; it is also the index of true global strategic reach.

The dominant strategic counter to maritime preponderance in the 21st century is Anti-Access / Area Denial (A2/AD): combinations of long-range anti-ship missiles, satellite surveillance, undersea sensors, mining, and submarine operations designed to make hostile waters too dangerous to enter at acceptable cost. China's DF-21D and DF-26 ballistic missiles — the "carrier killers" — are the textbook examples; Russia's Bastion coastal-defence system, Iran's swarm-of-small-boats doctrine in the Gulf, and North Korea's coastal artillery all operate on A2/AD logic.

The strategic consequence is that pure naval supremacy of the 1945 American kind is increasingly contested. The US Navy's Distributed Maritime Operations doctrine, the Marines' refocusing on island-chain warfare in the Pacific, and the AUKUS submarine partnership with Australia and the UK are all responses to a maritime environment in which the open commons cannot be assumed and chokepoints are increasingly inside other powers' weapons-engagement zones. The maritime balance of power is, on most readings, the central strategic question of the next two decades.

title: Resource Geopolitics
description: Oil, gas, water, rare earths, food — the politics of scarcity and supply

concepts.title: Oil and the 20th Century
concepts.contentHtml:
If a single commodity defined 20th-century geopolitics, it was oil. Naval transition from coal to oil before the First World War made petroleum a strategic necessity; the discovery of giant Middle Eastern fields in the 1920s–1950s reshaped the political map; and OPEC's 1973 embargo demonstrated that resource leverage could change global economic and political alignments overnight.

The structural facts are still recognisable. Roughly 60% of global proven oil reserves sit in the Middle East. The Strait of Hormuz carries about a fifth of global oil. Russia, Saudi Arabia, and the United States have alternated as the world's largest producers; the US shale revolution after 2010 transformed America from net importer to net exporter and reshaped global supply dynamics. The petrodollar system — oil priced in dollars, recycled through US Treasuries — has been a structural feature of post-1971 international finance.

The energy transition is reshaping but not abolishing this picture. As 2026 unfolds, oil demand growth has slowed in OECD economies and surged in parts of Asia; OPEC+'s capacity to manage prices through coordinated cuts has been tested by US shale, Russian wartime sales, and intra-cartel disputes. Gas — particularly LNG — has overtaken pipeline gas as a flexible global market, driven heavily by post-2022 European demand. Whatever the long-run trajectory, hydrocarbons remain the largest single source of state revenue for around two dozen countries, with all the strategic consequences that implies.

concepts.title: Critical Minerals and the New Resource Race
concepts.contentHtml:
The energy transition is not eliminating resource geopolitics; it is changing which resources matter. Lithium, cobalt, nickel, copper, graphite, and the rare-earth elements are the inputs of batteries, wind turbines, solar panels, and electric vehicles, and demand for them is forecast to multiply through the 2030s.

Their geographic distribution is highly uneven and politically consequential. The Democratic Republic of the Congo produces around 70% of the world's cobalt, much of it under hazardous conditions including child labour. Indonesia and the Philippines dominate nickel. Chile, Australia, and Argentina's "Lithium Triangle" account for most of global lithium reserves. China dominates the processing and refining of nearly all of these — a chokehold less in the mines than in the chemistry that turns raw ore into battery-grade material.

The strategic responses are recognisable. The US Inflation Reduction Act (2022) ties EV tax credits to North-American or allied-country sourcing. The EU Critical Raw Materials Act (2023) sets domestic production and recycling targets. Japan, after Chinese rare-earth export restrictions in 2010, deliberately diversified supply through investment in Australia and Vietnam. The pattern echoes the 1970s oil crises: a sudden recognition that key inputs sit in a small number of jurisdictions, followed by policy programmes to diversify supply, build strategic stockpiles, and develop substitutes. The current race is the energy-transition era's equivalent of OPEC.

concepts.title: Water, Food, and the Politics of Scarcity
concepts.contentHtml:
Beyond extracted commodities sit the slower-moving but potentially more consequential resources: water and food.

Most major rivers cross borders. The Nile (Ethiopia, Sudan, Egypt) has produced sustained tension over Ethiopia's GERD dam; the Tigris-Euphrates (Turkey, Syria, Iraq) is shaped by Turkish dam-building upstream; the Mekong (China, Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam) reflects the impact of Chinese upstream dams on downstream fisheries and agriculture; the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) between India and Pakistan has held through three wars but is increasingly stressed by climate change and political tension. The general pattern: upstream states have leverage their downstream neighbours rarely accept, and treaties are slow to adjust to new pressures.

Food security is the cumulative result. Ukraine and Russia together produce around a quarter of global wheat exports; the 2022 invasion produced food-price spikes that reverberated through North African and Middle Eastern politics in ways comparable to the 2008 commodity-price shock that helped trigger the Arab Spring. Climate change is reshaping the geography of agricultural production, with consequences (heat, drought, flooding) for breadbaskets in South Asia, the US Midwest, and the Sahel that are still being mapped.

Resource geopolitics is, in the end, a reminder that beyond all the doctrinal arguments about realism, liberalism, and constructivism sits a hard substrate: states with the resources their economies need do better, on average, than states without; states whose neighbours control upstream rivers, downstream straits, or refining plants, live with a permanent vulnerability. Geography, in this sense, never fully retires.

title: Great Power Competition
description: Hegemony, balancing, bandwagoning — the structure of multipolar rivalry

concepts.title: Polarity: Unipolar, Bipolar, Multipolar
concepts.contentHtml:
The structure of an international system is most often described by its polarity: how many great powers it contains. The post-1945 world has, on most readings, passed through three configurations.

The early Cold War was bipolar: two superpowers (US and USSR) dwarfing all others, with allies organised primarily around their alignment with one or the other. Kenneth Waltz argued in Theory of International Politics (1979) that bipolarity was unusually stable because each side could focus all its attention on a single rival, miscalculation was less likely than in multi-actor systems, and the alliance machinery was simpler.

The 1991–roughly-2008 period was unipolar: the United States as the sole superpower, with the EU and a recovering Russia as secondary actors and an emerging China not yet at full great-power scale. William Wohlforth's "Stability of a Unipolar World" (1999) argued that the US's overwhelming material advantage would deter balancing and produce a more cooperative system; subsequent events tested that hypothesis.

The 2010s and 2020s have produced what most analysts now call a multipolar or, more cautiously, a bipolar-tending system: US and China as the two largest actors, with the EU, Russia, India, and a rising tier of middle powers (Brazil, Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, South Africa) commanding distinct spheres of influence and increasingly willing to act independently of either superpower. The transition is contested in detail; that the unipolar moment has ended is no longer seriously argued.

concepts.title: Balancing, Bandwagoning, Buck-Passing, and Hedging
concepts.contentHtml:
What states do in response to great-power competition is the central object of structural-realist theory. Several recurring strategies have been formalised.

Balancing: aligning with weaker states against the most threatening one. Stephen Walt's Origins of Alliances (1987) argued, refining Kenneth Waltz, that states balance not against capability per se but against threat — a function of capability, geographic proximity, offensive intent, and offensive capability. NATO's expansion eastward, ASEAN's hedging against China, and Saudi Arabia's tilt toward the US during peak Iranian power all illustrate balancing logic.

Bandwagoning: aligning with the strongest threat, in hopes of reward or to avoid punishment. Many of the regimes that followed Hitler in 1939–40 (Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria) bandwagoned, as did some Arab states with Saudi Arabia in the 2010s. Bandwagoning is most attractive when balancing seems hopeless or when the dominant power offers concrete rewards.

Buck-passing: trying to get other states to balance the threat for you. Britain and France's stance toward Hitler in 1936–38 is the classical case. Hedging is the contemporary mixed strategy: maintaining productive relations with both blocs while quietly preparing to swing if the balance shifts. Many of the world's most important middle powers — India, Indonesia, Brazil, even Saudi Arabia and Turkey — are deliberately hedging in the current US–China competition rather than committing to either side.

concepts.title: Power Transitions and the Thucydides Trap
concepts.contentHtml:
One of the most-discussed concepts in contemporary great-power politics is the power transition framework. Going back to A. F. K. Organski's World Politics (1958), the argument is that the most dangerous moments in international politics are when a rising power approaches parity with the established hegemon — the established power feels its position eroding, the rising power feels its rights are being denied, and the structural pressure for war intensifies.

The popular version, owed to Graham Allison's Destined for War (2017), is the "Thucydides Trap": Allison studied 16 historical cases of major rising-power challenges since 1500 and found that 12 ended in war. The phrase echoes Thucydides's claim that the underlying cause of the Peloponnesian War was "the growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Sparta."

The application to the US–China contest is obvious — and contested. Skeptics (Joseph Nye, more cautiously G. John Ikenberry) note that economic interdependence, nuclear weapons, and dense institutional ties make a US–China war much costlier than past transitions. Pessimists (John Mearsheimer most prominently) argue that those features have been overstated as restraints, and that the structural pressure of the transition will overwhelm them. Allison's own conclusion is more pragmatic than the headline frame: war is not inevitable, but avoiding it requires deliberate, sustained statecraft of a kind neither Washington nor Beijing has so far demonstrated. The argument is one of the central frames of current US–China analysis.

title: Eurasia: Russia, Europe & Central Asia
description: From the EU to the Russian near abroad — the politics of the world-island

concepts.title: The European Project
concepts.contentHtml:
The European Union is the most ambitious experiment in pooled sovereignty in modern history. Founded as the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951 — six countries (France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg) sharing authority over the war-fighting industries — it has grown into a 27-member union with a single market, a common currency for 20 of those members, a functioning court (the CJEU), and a partial common foreign and defence policy.

The EU is genuinely a geopolitical actor in some domains and not in others. It is the world's largest single market by some measures, the world's regulatory superpower (the "Brussels effect," in Anu Bradford's phrase: GDPR, the Digital Markets Act, the AI Act all set de-facto global standards), and a major trade negotiator. It is much less of an actor in hard security: NATO, not the EU, has been the primary defence framework for European members since 1949.

The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine forced a revision. Germany announced a Zeitenwende in defence spending; Finland and Sweden joined NATO; a previously cautious EU has become the central supplier of financial, weapons, and political support for Ukraine. Whether the EU's strategic awakening persists or recedes is one of the central questions of European geopolitics.

concepts.title: Russia and the 'Near Abroad'
concepts.contentHtml:
Russian strategic thinking has been shaped, since 1991, around the concept of the "near abroad" — the post-Soviet states that Russia regards as falling within its sphere of legitimate influence. The view is contested by the states themselves, several of which have moved decisively westward, and by the West, which has consistently rejected sphere-of-influence claims as incompatible with the Helsinki principles of European security.

Russian behaviour in the near abroad has been escalatory. The 1991 dissolution left frozen conflicts in Transnistria, Abkhazia, South Ossetia, and Nagorno-Karabakh. The 2008 war with Georgia, the 2014 annexation of Crimea and intervention in eastern Ukraine, the 2020 backing of Lukashenko in Belarus, and the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine all illustrate the same pattern: Russia uses force or coercion to prevent post-Soviet states from definitively aligning westward.

The strategic case Russia has consistently made — that NATO expansion was a unilateral US move into Russia's security space — is contested by historians (the 1990 Baker–Gorbachev exchange about not expanding "one inch eastward" is read in opposing ways) and by the post-1991 Eastern European states, who chose to join NATO precisely because they read Russian behaviour as predictably aggressive. The 2022 invasion has, as a side-effect, validated the latter reading and probably ended the broader argument: NATO has reinforced rather than retreated, Sweden and Finland have joined, and Russia's strategic position in Europe is materially weaker than it was in 2021.

concepts.title: Central Asia and the Wider Eurasian Game
concepts.contentHtml:
The five Central Asian states — Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan — sit at the geographic centre of Mackinder's Heartland and are the object of overlapping competition.

Russia retains political and security ties through the Collective Security Treaty Organization, the Eurasian Economic Union, and Russian-language media; Russian troops were dispatched to Kazakhstan in January 2022 to support President Tokayev during unrest, in what was framed as a CSTO operation.

China has been the rising influence. The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (founded 2001) gives Beijing a regional security framework; the Belt and Road Initiative (announced in Astana, Kazakhstan, in 2013) has poured tens of billions of dollars of infrastructure financing into Central Asian railways, pipelines, and special economic zones. China has displaced Russia as the largest trading partner for most Central Asian states.

Other actors crowd in. Turkey has built influence through pan-Turkic cultural ties and the Organisation of Turkic States. India participates in the SCO and runs the Chabahar port project in Iran. Iran shares borders with Turkmenistan and competes for regional influence. The Central Asian republics themselves have become increasingly skilled at multi-vector foreign policy — taking infrastructure from China, security guarantees from Russia, and trade from Europe and Turkey, while resisting full alignment with any single power. This is the world-island's centre as it actually operates: not Mackinder's pivot ruled by a single hegemon but a contested zone of overlapping influences.

title: Indo-Pacific & East Asia
description: China's rise, Taiwan, Korea, ASEAN — the contested maritime arc

concepts.title: China's Rise and the Reshaping of East Asia
concepts.contentHtml:
The single most important geopolitical development of the past four decades is the rise of China. From under 2% of world GDP at the start of Deng Xiaoping's reforms in 1978, China grew to roughly 18% of world GDP by the mid-2020s, a manufacturing scale that exceeds the next nine countries combined, and a navy that has overtaken the US Navy in number of hulls (though not yet in tonnage or capability per ship).

The Chinese Communist Party's Belt and Road Initiative (announced 2013) has financed infrastructure projects in over 140 countries, with cumulative commitments around $1 trillion through 2024. Critics call it a debt-trap; defenders note that most loans have been restructured rather than seized, and that BRI fills genuine infrastructure gaps. Either way, BRI represents the most ambitious peacetime infrastructure programme any state has attempted.

Within East Asia, China's economic gravity has reshaped the region. South Korea, Japan, Taiwan, Australia, and most of ASEAN now trade more with China than with the US — even as their security ties remain tightly with Washington. The resulting double exposure — economic to Beijing, military to Washington — is the structural condition shaping much regional decision-making, and the central reason most regional states avoid framing their position as a choice between the two superpowers.

concepts.title: Taiwan, the Korean Peninsula, and the South China Sea
concepts.contentHtml:
Three regional flashpoints concentrate the strategic risk.

Taiwan is the most consequential. The PRC claims it as a renegade province; the ROC government has functioned independently since 1949; the US maintains strategic ambiguity through the Taiwan Relations Act (1979). The island is the world's largest producer of advanced semiconductors (TSMC alone produces around 60% of global wafer foundry by value, and over 90% of the most advanced chips), making it economically central to global technology supply chains. Chinese military exercises around Taiwan have intensified since 2022; US analysts assess Beijing wants to be ready for a Taiwan operation by the late 2020s, though whether war is intended is an open question.

The Korean peninsula remains technically at war (the 1953 armistice was never converted into a peace treaty). North Korea has built a nuclear-weapons capability and an ICBM that can reach the continental United States; South Korea's response includes a massive missile-defence build-up and recurring debates about its own nuclear option.

The South China Sea has been transformed since 2014 by Chinese island-building on disputed reefs in the Spratlys and Paracels — runways, ports, and missile sites on artificial islands. The 2016 ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration that China's "nine-dash line" has no basis in international law was rejected by Beijing. Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, and Indonesia all have overlapping claims; the Philippines under President Marcos has tilted sharply toward closer US alignment in response.

concepts.title: ASEAN and the Quad: Architectures of the Indo-Pacific
concepts.contentHtml:
The regional institutional architecture has multiplied. ASEAN (founded 1967) brings together 10 Southeast Asian states; its central principle is consensus and non-interference, and its preferred mode is dialogue rather than confrontation. ASEAN has resisted being forced to take sides in the US–China contest, and its central forum (the East Asia Summit) deliberately includes both.

Newer arrangements are more US-aligned. The Quad (Australia, India, Japan, US) reactivated in 2017 and has held summits regularly since 2021. The AUKUS security partnership (2021), under which the US and UK help Australia acquire nuclear-powered submarines, was widely read as a pivot in Australian strategic alignment. Bilateral US alliances with Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Thailand, and Australia remain the spine of the regional security architecture; Japan and South Korea have tentatively reopened cooperation since 2023 despite long-running historical tensions.

The region's central strategic question is the same one Spykman would have recognised: can the US and its allies sustain a Rimland posture along the Indo-Pacific arc against rising Chinese capability and economic gravity? The answer, in the 2020s, is increasingly conditional — depending on US political continuity, allied burden-sharing, and Chinese choices. The Indo-Pacific is the region where great-power competition is most live, the costs of miscalculation highest, and the institutional restraints — UN Security Council, international law, regional consensus — weakest.

title: Middle East & North Africa
description: Sectarianism, oil, proxy wars — the geopolitics of a fractured region

concepts.title: From Ottoman Empire to Sykes-Picot to Modern States
concepts.contentHtml:
Most of the modern Middle East was, until 1918, part of the Ottoman Empire. The carving up of those territories during and after the First World War — through the secret Sykes-Picot Agreement (1916) between Britain and France, the Balfour Declaration (1917) on a Jewish homeland, the League of Nations Mandates (1922) — created the borders that, with adjustments, define the region today.

The borders ran across communal, sectarian, and tribal divisions. Modern Iraq, Syria, Jordan, Lebanon, and Israel/Palestine were drawn for the convenience of European powers rather than the cohesion of the populations within them. Iraq's Sunni-Shia-Kurdish composition, Syria's Alawite-Sunni-Druze-Kurdish-Christian mosaic, and Lebanon's confessional system are colonial-era inheritances that have shaped every subsequent conflict.

The post-1945 history added new layers. The 1948 establishment of Israel and the Arab-Israeli wars that followed; the 1953 CIA-British coup against Mossadegh in Iran; the 1979 Iranian Revolution; the 1980–88 Iran-Iraq war; the 1990–91 Gulf War; the 2003 US-led invasion of Iraq; the 2011 Arab Spring; the Syrian civil war; the rise and fall of ISIS; the post-2023 Gaza war; the 2024–25 collapse of the Assad regime in Syria — each event has reshaped the regional order in ways that the Sykes-Picot states' fragile institutions struggle to absorb.

concepts.title: Sectarianism, Saudi-Iran Rivalry, and Proxy Wars
concepts.contentHtml:
The dominant inter-state rivalry of the 21st-century Middle East has been between Saudi Arabia (Sunni-majority, monarchical, conservative, US-aligned) and Iran (Shia-majority, revolutionary, theocratic, anti-US). The rivalry is partly sectarian — invoking historical Sunni-Shia divides — and partly geopolitical: two regional powers contesting influence across a fractured region.

The contest plays out almost exclusively through proxies. Iran has built the "Axis of Resistance": Hezbollah in Lebanon, the Assad regime in Syria (until 2024), various Iraqi Shia militias, the Houthis in Yemen, and Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza. Saudi Arabia has supported Sunni governments and rebel groups in Syria, financed factions in Yemen's civil war, and maintained close ties with Egypt, Jordan, and the Gulf monarchies. The 2023 Chinese-brokered Saudi-Iranian normalisation reduced rather than eliminated the tension; the 2023–24 Israel-Hamas war and Israel's parallel campaigns against Hezbollah and the Houthis put the proxy network under unprecedented stress.

The wider regional pattern of state weakness means that proxy contests do not just escalate inter-state rivalries — they tear the host states apart. Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, Iraq, and Libya have all suffered prolonged civil wars in which external sponsors fueled and prolonged conflicts that the domestic political systems could not resolve. The cumulative human cost is among the largest of any region in the post-1945 period.

concepts.title: Oil, the US Pivot, and the Future of the Region
concepts.contentHtml:
The Middle East has been, since 1945, the world's largest source of exportable oil and (more recently) gas. US engagement with the region began under Roosevelt's 1945 meeting with Saudi King Abdulaziz on the USS Quincy — establishing a security-for-oil relationship that lasted, in modified form, for decades. The Carter Doctrine (1980) committed the US to defending Persian Gulf access by force; the 1991 Gulf War and the 2003 Iraq invasion can be read partly through that lens.

The US position has been shifting. The shale revolution made the US a net exporter of oil and gas; American attention has pivoted toward the Indo-Pacific; the US is no longer willing to lead military operations on the scale of the 2003 Iraq War. The 2020 Abraham Accords normalising relations between Israel and the UAE, Bahrain, and Morocco shifted regional alignments in ways that suited US strategic preferences (a Sunni-Israeli understanding aligned against Iran) without requiring direct US deployments.

Other powers have moved in. China has become the largest customer for Saudi, Emirati, and Iranian oil; brokered the 2023 Saudi-Iran normalisation; and built deep economic ties without a comparable security commitment. Russia has sustained its Syrian foothold through the Assad regime and active military presence (now reduced by Assad's fall). Turkey under Erdoğan has pursued neo-Ottoman influence projects in Syria, Libya, and the eastern Mediterranean. The result is the Middle East's first multipolar moment in decades — less American, more contested, and more dangerous in some respects than the unipolar period it has replaced.

title: The US–China Contest
description: Decoupling, tech war, Thucydides trap — the defining rivalry of the century

concepts.title: From Engagement to Strategic Competition
concepts.contentHtml:
For three decades after Deng Xiaoping's reforms, US policy toward China was built on engagement: integrate China into the global economy and into multilateral institutions on the assumption that prosperity and interdependence would moderate Chinese behaviour and, eventually, its political system. The 2001 Chinese accession to the WTO, normalised trade relations, and broad academic and corporate ties all expressed that bet.

By the late 2010s, the bipartisan US consensus had concluded that the bet had failed. Xi Jinping's consolidation of personal power, the militarisation of the South China Sea, the crushing of Hong Kong's autonomy, the mass detention of Uighurs in Xinjiang, and the steady displacement of US firms by state-backed Chinese rivals in strategic sectors all contributed to the shift. The 2017 US National Security Strategy formally identified China as a "strategic competitor"; the language has been bipartisan since.

Chinese strategic thinking has run on a parallel track. The CCP's emphasis on "great changes unseen in a century" (Xi's 2018 phrase), on technological self-reliance, and on a Chinese-led international order is built on a reading of the US as a declining hegemon attempting to constrain a rising power. Each side now treats the relationship as primarily competitive; the question is how that competition is managed.

concepts.title: The Tech War and Decoupling
concepts.contentHtml:
The most active front of the US–China contest is technological. From 2018 onward, the US has used export controls, investment restrictions, and sanctions to constrain Chinese access to advanced technology — initially under Trump (Huawei sanctions, ZTE restrictions), then expanded substantially under Biden (the October 2022 chip export controls, additional measures in 2023 and 2024) and continued under Trump's second term.

The semiconductor industry has become the central battleground. The US, the Netherlands (where ASML produces the EUV lithography machines without which advanced chips cannot be made), Japan, and South Korea have coordinated to deny China access to leading-edge chip production capability. China has responded with massive subsidies for domestic semiconductor manufacturing (the "Made in China 2025" programme and successors), partial workarounds, and counter-restrictions on rare-earth exports critical to chip production elsewhere.

The broader process is decoupling in some sectors and de-risking in others. The European Union's preferred phrase, "de-risking, not decoupling," captures the tension: nobody wants a full economic divorce that would impose enormous costs, but everyone now treats supply-chain concentration in single-jurisdiction risk as unacceptable in strategic sectors. Whether this produces parallel technology stacks (the "splinternet," extended), a managed coexistence, or a more aggressive cold-war-style separation is the central commercial question of the next decade.

concepts.title: Taiwan, the Thucydides Trap, and the Limits of Analogy
concepts.contentHtml:
The most dangerous flashpoint is Taiwan. The PRC's official position is that reunification is non-negotiable; the use of force is reserved as a last resort but explicitly not renounced. The US's Taiwan Relations Act (1979) commits the US to providing Taiwan with the means to defend itself and to opposing unilateral changes to the status quo — but is deliberately ambiguous about whether the US would itself fight. The combination of Taiwan's strategic significance (semiconductors, geographic position in the first island chain, democratic government) and the PRC's stated intent makes it the highest-risk single scenario in great-power politics.

The framework most often used to assess US–China prospects is Graham Allison's Thucydides Trap: 12 of 16 historical rising-power challenges since 1500 ended in war. Sceptics emphasise the moderating factors absent from past cases — nuclear deterrence, deep economic interdependence, dense institutional contacts. Pessimists note that nuclear weapons did not prevent the Cuban Missile Crisis from coming within hours of launch, and that economic interdependence did not prevent 1914.

The realistic policy frame is neither inevitable war nor a return to engagement but managed competition: maintaining military deterrence, building economic resilience, sustaining alliance commitments, and constructing the diplomatic channels and crisis-management mechanisms that can prevent escalation when (not if) crises occur. Whether the political systems on both sides — populist polarisation in the US, personalist authoritarianism in China — can sustain that level of disciplined statecraft over decades is the deeper question. The 21st-century international order will be shaped by the answer.
